Chapter 4: Openness to Mystery—Living with Unknowing.
You know, there's a real sense of relief when we finally admit that not everything in this world is meant to be understood. Have you ever noticed how forcing ourselves to find answers for every question can just leave us frustrated or disappointed?
But what if there’s another way—a way that actually welcomes mystery, and finds peace in the simple act of not knowing?
I’m reminded of a story. A student, determined to master every last detail, once came to a wise mentor with a list of questions as long as their arm. The mentor listened quietly, then suggested they take a walk out in the garden. As they wandered among the trees, the mentor pointed to the sunlight flickering through the leaves and the wind weaving its way through the branches.
“See how everything’s alive, even if you can’t explain exactly how?” the mentor asked. And in that moment, the student realized—some things are meant to be experienced, not explained.
This kind of openness to mystery sits at the heart of both Asian spirituality and the teachings of Christ. In many Eastern traditions, the unknown isn’t something to fear—it’s something to embrace. The Tao, for instance, is described as something you can’t really put a name to or grasp, but it’s present in everything.
And think about how often Christ spoke in parables—stories that invite us to wonder, reflect, and leave room for questions.
Most of us grow up being taught to seek certainty, to chase down answers, and to steer clear of anything ambiguous. But let’s be honest—life rarely plays along. Plans unravel, expectations fall short, and the future stubbornly refuses to reveal itself. In those moments, the real invitation isn’t to panic or give up. It’s to trust—to believe that, even in the middle of confusion, there’s a deeper wisdom quietly at work.
Picture a family facing an uncertain future. They’re sitting around the dinner table, the air heavy with worry and “what ifs.” But as the evening goes on, something shifts. Laughter bubbles up. Old stories get shared. For a little while, that burden of uncertainty feels lighter. And suddenly, it’s clear—joy and connection don’t depend on having all the answers.
The teachings of Christ really encourage this kind of trust. He didn’t hand out blueprints for every situation. Instead, he invited people to live with open hearts. “Don’t worry about tomorrow,” he said. Not because tomorrow isn’t important—but because life is happening right here, right now. And in the East, we find a similar message in the practice of mindfulness—the art of being fully present, moment to moment.
Openness to mystery doesn’t mean giving up on understanding. It means recognizing the limits of what we know, and being willing to learn from what we can’t explain. It’s a kind of humility—the courage to admit we don’t have all the answers, and to see that as a gift, not a failure.
There’s a wonderful example of this in science. Imagine a scientist who’s spent years deep in research, only to discover that every answer leads to even more questions. But instead of getting frustrated, they feel a sense of awe. The universe turns out to be bigger and more beautiful than they ever imagined. And maybe, the mystery of Christ is a little bit like that too—not a problem to solve, but a reality to live.
Living this way takes real courage. It means letting go of the need to control everything. It means trusting that even the unknown can bring about something good. It asks us to wait, to listen, to be open to surprise. And to believe that—even in the darkest moments—there’s still light to be found.
Openness to mystery isn’t about passively resigning ourselves. It’s about actively engaging with life. It’s the willingness to show up, to be present, to receive whatever comes with an open heart. Because in the end, the greatest truths aren’t the ones we can explain—they’re the ones we get to live, day by day.
